oneSentence: Three vectors produced by learned projections represent matching needs, matching features, and information that attention may pass onward.
plainExplanation:
In a transformer, each token first has a vector, which is a list of numbers representing features. From that token representation, the model creates three different versions: a query, a key and a value. They are related, but they do different jobs.

The query represents features used to seek relevant context. The key represents features used for matching. The value represents information that may be passed onward. The model compares one token’s query with other tokens’ keys to produce compatibility scores. A normalising step turns these scores into attention weights.

Those weights are then used to mix the value vectors. So the output is not the key or the value from one place only. It is usually a weighted combination of many values, with larger weights on tokens whose keys matched the query more strongly. This is how a token representation incorporates context from other tokens.

These three vectors are often confused with search systems because the words sound similar. But here they are internal projections inside the model, not database fields. They are also not fixed meanings attached to words forever. Their numbers depend on the learned projections, the layer, the attention head and the input representation.

everydayAnalogy.title: Sorting survey comments by the issue they raise
everydayAnalogy.story: A team receives hundreds of short survey comments from people in Nairobi, Lima and Sarajevo. For each comment, the team writes one short note about what issue they are trying to identify, one label card listing the issues the comment might relate to, and one fuller summary card with the useful details from that comment. To group comments, they compare the issue note from one comment with the label cards on all comments. Comments with stronger matches contribute more of their summary cards to the final grouped view.

mapping.analogyElement: stronger or weaker match between note and label card
mapping.aiElement: attention score used as a weight

everydayAnalogy.limitation: In the analogy, people write readable notes and labels on purpose. In a transformer, the vectors are lists of numbers learned during training, and humans usually cannot read a single dimension as a clear label. Also, the real mechanism works in many layers and heads at once, and it combines values numerically rather than physically sorting cards into piles.

visual.title: How query, key and value produce contextual output
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to explain that attention compares queries with keys to get weights, then uses those weights to mix values.
visual.description: Show one current token on the left and several context tokens on the right. Each token splits into Q, K and V boxes. Arrows go from the current token’s Q to all K boxes, then to score circles, then to weighted arrows into the V boxes, and finally to one combined output box. Read left to right.

steps.label: 1. Start from token representations
steps.explanation: Each token already has a vector representation from the model. A small learned linear transform turns that representation into three versions: Q, K and V.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw four token rectangles in one row. Under each, show three small stacked boxes labelled Q, K and V. Use one colour family per token and consistent labels.

steps.label: 2. The current token forms a query
steps.explanation: For the token being updated, the model uses its query as a request for relevant context.
steps.visualInstruction: Highlight the first token as the current token. Emphasise its Q box with a thicker outline. Fade the Q boxes of the other tokens slightly.

steps.label: 3. Compare query with keys
steps.explanation: The current query is compared with every token’s key, including often its own key. These comparisons produce attention scores: higher means a closer match for this head and layer.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw arrows from the highlighted Q box to every K box. Place a score circle on each arrow with example labels such as 0.1, 0.6, 0.2, 0.1.

steps.label: 4. Use scores to weight values
steps.explanation: The scores become weights. Tokens with larger weights contribute more of their value vectors.
steps.visualInstruction: From each score circle, draw an arrow to the matching V box, then onward toward a merge area. Make thicker arrows for larger scores.

steps.label: 5. Combine values into output
steps.explanation: The weighted values are added together to form one contextual output vector for the current token.
steps.visualInstruction: Merge all weighted V arrows into one output rectangle labelled contextual output for current token. Add a note that this output is passed to later layers or steps.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, each arrow from Q to K highlights its score and the matching contribution from V to the output; a toggle switches between numeric example weights and plain-language labels such as low, medium and high.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram explains attention for one token. First, each token has three derived vectors called query, key and value. Second, the current token’s query is compared with every token’s key to produce scores. Third, those scores are used as weights on the corresponding value vectors. Fourth, the weighted value vectors are combined into one output vector for the current token. The key idea is that keys are used for matching, while values are used for the information that gets mixed into the output.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static left-to-right diagram shows token vectors split into Q, K and V, then arrows from one query to all keys, score labels above those arrows, thicker weighted arrows from values, and one final combined output box.

workedExample.scenario: While checking a pilot’s draft lessons-learned note, an evaluation officer examines how one attention head updates “it” in the simplified token sequence: “The pilot revised the workplan because it was incomplete.”
workedExample.input: Illustrative attention weights from “it” to every token: The 0.03, pilot 0.10, revised 0.05, the 0.02, workplan 0.55, because 0.05, it 0.05, was 0.05, incomplete 0.10.
process: The head projects the representation of “it” into a query. It separately projects every token’s representation into a key and a value using learned matrices.
It compares the query for “it” with every key, scales the resulting compatibility scores and applies softmax, producing weights that sum to 1.
The key for “workplan” receives the largest weight, 0.55. This controls how much of the corresponding value vector enters the output, but it does not mean the key and value vectors are identical.

The contextual output is the weighted sum of all value vectors: 0.03×V(The) + 0.10×V(pilot) + 0.05×V(revised) + 0.02×V(the) + 0.55×V(workplan) + 0.05×V(because) + 0.05×V(it) + 0.05×V(was) + 0.10×V(incomplete).
workedExample.result: For this attention head, the value vector at “workplan” makes the largest contribution to the updated representation of “it”. Other heads may attend differently, and later layers combine those outputs before the model produces any text.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: An evaluation officer at a Geneva duty station is finalising the lessons-learned note from a pilot before close of business. Progress reports arrived in Arabic, English and French. In an approved multilingual model, each token produces query, key and value vectors. A query from a pronoun, for example, may match strongly with the key of an earlier noun, causing that noun’s value vector to contribute more to the pronoun’s contextual representation.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The mechanism helps the evaluation officer understand how the model connects related words across a sentence when summarising findings from reports in several languages. It also explains why attention is not a database lookup: learned similarities determine a weighted blend of value vectors.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Attention weights do not prove why the model produced a conclusion and should not be treated as an evaluation finding. Raw interview notes, names or details that could identify participants must not be entered into a tool unless it is authorised for that material, because evaluation records may contain confidential personal information. Outputs still require review against the source reports.

whyItMatters: If you hear that a transformer uses attention, query, key and value are the parts that make that mechanism work. Knowing their roles helps you judge system behaviour more clearly. You can ask better questions: what is being matched, what information is being passed forward, and why might the model focus on the wrong context? This matters when reading model cards, debugging failures, comparing architectures, or deciding whether a system is suitable for tasks like summarisation, translation or image analysis. It also helps separate a real mechanism from marketing language: the model is not searching a database in a human sense, but computing weighted combinations of internal vectors.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Query, key and value are three different kinds of data stored in a model like fields in a database.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are not database columns. They are learned vector projections created from token representations inside an attention layer. Their job is computational: queries are used for matching, keys for being matched against, and values for providing the content that gets combined.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The model picks one value from one token and copies it into the output.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Usually it does not make a single hard choice. Attention normally produces a weighted mixture of many value vectors. One token may dominate, but several tokens can contribute at the same time, which is why the output can reflect blended context.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A key stores meaning and a value stores facts, so they are stable across all contexts.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Keys and values are context-dependent internal representations, not permanent labelled containers. Their exact numbers depend on the layer, the attention head, the surrounding tokens and the learned weights. A token can produce different useful patterns in different contexts.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Query, key and value only matter in text models.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The same mechanism appears in many transformer-based systems, including language, vision, speech and multimodal models. The items being related may be words, image patches, audio frames or other units, but the matching-and-mixing idea is similar.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: The model derives three vectors from each token representation: one used to seek matches, one used for matching, and one containing information that may be combined.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Given an input representation x for each token, an attention head applies three learned linear projections to produce q = xW_Q, k = xW_K and v = xW_V. For one token position, its query is compared with all keys, often by a dot product, to produce raw compatibility scores. After scaling and a normalising step such as softmax, these become attention weights. The head then computes a weighted sum of the value vectors using those weights, yielding a contextualised output for that position. In self-attention, q, k and v all come from the same sequence; in cross-attention, the query comes from one sequence or stream while keys and values come from another. The important distinction is functional: keys determine matching, values determine what information is aggregated.

keyTakeaway: A query tests what the current position should match, keys determine the strength of each match, and values supply the information blended into the contextual output.

quickCheck.question: In an attention head, what is the main role of the value vector?
options: It stores the final probability of the next token.
It is the information weighted and combined after query-key matching.
It decides the position of the token in the sequence.
It replaces the embedding so the model no longer needs token vectors.
quickCheck.explanation: Queries and keys are mainly used to compute matching scores. Values are the vectors that get multiplied by the resulting weights and summed to form the contextual output. So values carry the content that attention passes forward.

issues.problem: The story shifts from comparing one comment’s query with all keys to producing a single "final grouped view". Attention normally produces a separate contextual output for each query, not one global grouping of all comments.
issues.fix: A team receives hundreds of short survey comments from people in Nairobi, Lima and Sarajevo. For each comment, the team writes one short note about what related information it needs, one label card listing what the comment may match, and one fuller summary card with useful details. For one comment, they compare its issue note with the label cards on all comments. Stronger matches contribute more of their summary cards to the contextual view for that comment.

issues.problem: The visual labels examples such as 0.1, 0.6, 0.2 and 0.1 as comparison scores, then says scores simply become weights. The page’s technical account correctly says raw compatibility scores require scaling and normalisation before they are weights.
issues.fix: In step 3, call the comparison results raw compatibility scores. Insert scaling and normalisation before step 4, or label the displayed numbers attention weights after normalisation. Change step 4 to: "Use the resulting weights on values. Tokens with larger weights contribute more of their value vectors."

issues.problem: The accessibility text repeats the score-weight conflation and therefore does not accurately describe the same mechanism as the technical explanation.
issues.fix: The diagram explains attention for one token. First, each token has three derived vectors called query, key and value. Second, the current token’s query is compared with every token’s key to produce compatibility scores. Third, scaling and normalisation turn those scores into weights on the corresponding value vectors. Fourth, the weighted value vectors are combined into one output vector for the current token. Keys are used for matching, while values provide the information mixed into the output.

issues.problem: The process says the query is compared with every token’s key, but the displayed weighted sum includes only four tokens and calls that the contextual output. The sentence also contains "The", "the", "because", "it" and "was". The four shown coefficients do sum correctly: 0.05 + 0.10 + 0.70 + 0.15 = 1.00. That leaves no weight for the omitted tokens, but the page never states that this is a simplified, renormalised four-token example.
issues.fix: State that this is a simplified calculation over four shown candidates. Replace the second process step with: "For this simplified example, it compares the query with four candidate keys and normalises their weights to sum to 1." Replace the fourth with: "For these four candidates, the weighted contribution is 0.05×V(city) + 0.10×V(approved) + 0.70×V(plan) + 0.15×V(urgent)."

issues.problem: A large contribution from the value at "plan" does not by itself establish that the model has resolved the pronoun as referring to the plan. Attention weights and value mixing are not a direct coreference decision.
issues.fix: In this head, the output for "it" receives its largest shown value contribution from "plan". Other heads and later layers may use this contextual information.

issues.problem: It presents tokens as literally asking and saying things. It also says each token makes the vectors, rather than saying the model derives them from the token representation.
issues.fix: The model derives three vectors from each token representation: one used to seek matches, one used for matching, and one containing information that may be combined.

issues.problem: "Queries choose where to look" anthropomorphises the mechanism and wrongly assigns the choice to the query alone. Attention weights result from comparisons between queries and keys.
issues.fix: Queries and keys determine matching weights, while values provide the information blended into the output.

issues.problem: Option 2 is the only correct answer, but the other options are implausible category errors. A reader can select the answer without understanding the distinction among query, key and value.
issues.fix: Use these options: ["It is compared with keys to produce compatibility scores.", "It is the information weighted and combined after query-key matching.", "It is matched against a query to help produce compatibility scores.", "It normalises the compatibility scores into weights."]. Keep correctOptionIndex as 1.
